case_study_insert.main_stem: Northvale Apparel (NVX) is a public limited company in the fashion clothing manufacturing and retail sector, employing a workforce of 96. Founded in 2008 by Sofia Northvale, the business designs, makes and sells own-label clothing for high-street and online customers and operates a hierarchical organisational structure with autocratic leadership. NVX plans to invest $640,000 in a new automated cutting and sewing line using responsible fabrics, financed by a $340,000 five-year bank loan and $300,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $168,000 a year, a variable cost of $7.20 a unit and a selling price of $12.00, and currently produces 80,000 units a year. NVX faces two operational problems: its garment-finishing defect rate has reached 4.2% and labour turnover on the production line is rising.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report â€” Q3 2025: The garment line stitched 21,600 units last quarter at a defect rate of 4.2%, down from 5.6% a year earlier. Customer complaints about sizing fell from 52 to 30 per month. Average order dispatch time is 3.4 days. A survey of 820 fashion shoppers found that 57% would pay up to $0.50 more for responsibly sourced clothing, and 49% check fabric labels before buying. A skills audit shows 24 of 96 production staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new automated cutters; an external course costs $110 per employee.

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.50% to 5.25%, increasing borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.2% from $13.20 to $14.02 per hour from April 2026, lifting wage bills in garments and warehousing. (3) Wholesale cotton and fabric costs have risen 11.3% year-on-year, consumer spending on clothing grew 1.8%, and retail inflation is running at 7.0%.

questions.question_text: NVX plans to fund part of its $640,000 expansion with a $340,000 five-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for NVX of using a $300,000 share issue instead.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A share issue raises $300,000 without interest charges or a fixed repayment date, so unlike the $340,000 bank loan it adds no debt service to NVX's costs. That protects the $4.80 contribution per unit on 80,000 units and helps fund a new automated cutting and sewing line using responsible fabrics even if fashion clothing manufacturing and retail demand softens.

Point 2: Equity finance also avoids the collateral and repossession risk of a bank loan, so the $640,000 investment is not jeopardised if trading deteriorates. To be a public company, NVX can sell shares to outside investors, widening the capital base beyond retained earnings. The trade-off is some dilution of existing shareholders' control, but for Sofia Northvale's business the absence of compulsory interest and repayment makes the share issue the safer foundation for a hierarchical organisation with 96 staff.

Taken together, the $300,000 funds a new automated cutting and sewing line using responsible fabrics without competing with the $340,000 debt service, leaving the $168,000 of annual fixed costs to be covered by the $4.80 contribution on each of the 80,000 units. In fashion clothing manufacturing and retail, where the 11.3% input-cost rise already pressures margins, avoiding compulsory interest payments gives NVX a materially safer route than increasing its borrowings for a hierarchical organisation with 96 staff.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to Northvale Apparel and its financing choice.

questions.question_text: NVX is promoting its fashion clothing manufacturing and retail offering. Consider television advertising, fashion magazine print advertising, or social media influencer marketing. Which should NVX choose to promote its new clothing line? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Television advertising: TV delivers mass reach and can quickly build national awareness of the new clothing line, which suits a public limited company selling through high-street and online channels. The cost of production and airtime is very high, and much of the audience is outside the target fashion segment, so wastage is large against a $640,000 expansion.

Fashion magazine print advertising: Print places the line in a credible, style-focused context and reaches readers interested in clothing. It is cheaper than television, but circulation is falling, deadlines are long and the message cannot be changed quickly; it also cannot be linked directly to online sales for NVX.

Social media influencer marketing: Influencers demonstrate garments to engaged followers and can be tracked to website visits, reaching the $0.50% of surveyed shoppers influenced by fabric and sourcing information. Costs are controllable, though outcomes rely on influencer credibility and take time to compound.

Recommendation: NVX should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches style-conscious, online fashion buyers at controllable cost and can be measured against website traffic, suiting a public limited company funding a $640,000 line. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted, and magazine print is rejected as declining, slow and unmeasurable for an online-linked clothing brand.

With fixed costs of $168,000 a year and a $340,000 loan to service, NVX needs volume at a controlled cost, so the chosen method must reach buyers who will actually convert; that is why the two rejected options, despite their superficial appeal, are set aside in favour of the more targeted approach. The decision should be reviewed against the sales and enquiry figures in Appendix 1 after one campaign cycle, and the spend justified only if the extra orders cover the $4.80 contribution needed toward the $168,000 fixed costs of the fashion clothing manufacturing and retail business.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge of promotional methods with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of the business with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of Northvale Apparel with a well-justified recommendation explaining why the two rejected options lose.

questions.question_text: NVX's defect rate is 4.2% and labour turnover is rising. Explain two benefits for NVX of using autocratic leadership on its garment line.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Autocratic leadership gives clear, firm instructions on cutting and sewing standards, which directly tackles the 4.2% garment-finishing defect rate. On a hierarchical fashion clothing manufacturing and retail line, a single decisive leader can enforce inspection routines quickly, so fewer faulty garments reach customers and the fall in complaints from 52 to 30 can continue.

Point 2: In a labour-turnover problem, autocratic leadership allows rapid reallocation of the 96 production staff and quick decisions on training with the new automated cutters, keeping output near 80,000 units. Clear expectations also reduce ambiguity for new recruits. Sofia Northvale must balance this with consultation, since overly directive control can lower morale in the long run, but for immediate quality and discipline it suits the situation.

These benefits matter because fixed costs of $168,000 mean NVX must keep output close to 80,000 units a year; every experienced worker lost through turnover or absence is replaced at a retraining cost shown in Appendix 1, and a destabilised team would slow the $640,000 rollout. Better motivation therefore protects the quality figures reported in Appendix 1 and the $4.80 contribution on each unit, which is what allows the public limited company to absorb the 11.3% rise in cotton and fabric costs without cutting the 80,000-unit plan.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to Northvale Apparel's problem, costs and output.

questions.question_text: NVX must train staff to use its new equipment. Consider on-the-job training on the automated cutters or an external course at $110 per employee. Which should NVX choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training on the automated cutters: Learning on the actual machines is directly relevant to NVX's 4.2% finishing-defect problem, costs no course fee, and keeps the 24 staff productive, protecting output of 80,000 units. Drawbacks are that trainers are production staff whose own work suffers and bad habits can be passed on, with little formal certification for a public limited company.

External course at $110 per employee: A structured external course gives up-to-date skills and a recognised qualification for all 24 staff, costing 24 Ã— $110 = $2,640, modest against the $640,000 line. It removes staff from the line temporarily and may be generic, so follow-up on site would still be needed.

Decision: NVX should choose on-the-job training on the cutters, with a short external course later for senior operators. On-the-job training is cheaper, machine-specific and protects output while the defect rate is high; the full external course is rejected because losing 24 staff from the line and paying $2,640 would disrupt the $640,000 expansion schedule.

The wider context reinforces this decision. With fixed costs of $168,000 and the $340,000 loan to service, NVX cannot afford the output loss that follows withdrawing the staff concerned from the line for long. The documented problem in Appendix 1 â€” the defect and turnover figures â€” makes early practical competence on the actual equipment more valuable than a generic certificate. A short external top-up later can add formal recognition without the disruption of full off-the-job training, so the chosen blend protects both the 80,000-unit volume and the quality the public limited company is trying to improve as it invests $640,000 in new fashion clothing manufacturing and retail capacity.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to the business.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of the business.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of Northvale Apparel with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how NVX's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs Ã· Contribution per unit. Substitution: $168,000 Ã· ($12.00 âˆ’ $7.20) = $168,000 Ã· $4.80 = 35,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 35,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price âˆ’ Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $12.00 âˆ’ $7.20 = $4.80. Answer: contribution per unit is $4.80.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways NVX's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 35,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 80,000 units, giving a margin of safety of 45,000 units, to judge whether the $640,000 investment is safely profitable.
2. Contribution per unit of $4.80 lets managers model a discount: for example a 5% cut in the $12.00 selling price would lower contribution and show the extra volume needed to cover $168,000 fixed costs.
3. With $168,000 fixed costs and $4.80 contribution, managers can set the sales volumes needed to service the $340,000 loan before committing further capital to a new automated cutting and sewing line using responsible fabrics.
4. Unit cost of about $9.30 ($168,000 Ã· 80,000 units + $7.20) can be benchmarked each quarter to spot waste from the cotton and fabric cost inflation of 11.3% and to check whether the $7.20 variable cost can be renegotiated. Together these figures guide pricing, volume and cost control at NVX.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 35,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $4.80 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 45,000 units against 80,000 output; pricing/discount modelling against $168,000 fixed costs; loan-service volume for the $640,000 expansion; and unit-cost benchmarking at about $9.30 to tackle 11.3% input-cost inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate NVX's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has NVX's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.26 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.29 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.56 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.72 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $140 inventories + $88 trade receivables + $24 cash = $252; 2025 current assets = $110 + $96 + $40 = $246. Dividing by current liabilities of $200 (2024) and $190 (2025) gives the 2024 figure of 1.26 and the 2025 figure of 1.29. For the second measure, (current assets âˆ’ inventories) Ã· current liabilities gives 2024: ($252 âˆ’ $140) Ã· $200 = $112 Ã· $200 = 0.56; 2025: ($246 âˆ’ $110) Ã· $190 = $136 Ã· $190 = 0.72.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened on both measures. The 2024 coverage of 1.26 rose to 1.29 in 2025, meaning current assets cover short-term obligations more comfortably, helped by current liabilities falling from $200 to $190. The stricter measure, which excludes inventories, improved from 0.56 to 0.72, so NVX is less dependent on selling stock to meet debts â€” important while it services a $340,000 loan and funds a $640,000 expansion. Trade receivables moved from $88 to $96, tying up cash that could be slower to collect, and inventories moved from $140 to $110, so availability for peak demand should still be watched. Non-current assets grew from $1,400 to $1,820, consistent with the new investment, while capital employed rose from $1,600 to $1,950.

Conclusion: NVX's financial position has improved. Both short-term solvency measures rose (1.26 to 1.29 and 0.56 to 0.72) and the improvement does not rely on inventory alone. The main residual risk is the $96 of trade receivables, so tighter credit control is advisable before further expansion.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether Northvale Apparel's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for NVX of switching to responsibly sourced fabric for its clothing line.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Responsible fabric aligns with the 57% of surveyed shoppers willing to pay $$0.50 more and the 49%% who check fabric labels, supporting a premium price that protects the $4.80 contribution per unit and helps win listings.

Disadvantage: Responsible fabrics usually cost more, which would raise the $7.20 variable cost; with input costs already up 49%, the margin could be squeezed unless the premium is accepted. Supply of certified fabric may also be less reliable, risking the 80,000-unit output.

Managers should set the premium against the $4.80 contribution per unit and the $168,000 annual fixed costs: the survey evidence in Appendix 1 suggests customers will pay more, but the 11.3% rise in cotton and fabric costs and the need to sustain 80,000 units mean the net gain must be checked. If volumes fall, the extra cost would not be recovered, so the effect should be reviewed after one quarter. For a public limited company with 96 staff, the change also affects training and the brand Sofia Northvale has built, so it belongs alongside the service and quality improvements already reported in Appendix 1 rather than being introduced in isolation.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to Northvale Apparel's data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.25%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase and the 11.3% rise in cotton and fabric input costs will affect NVX. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.50% to 5.25%): The insert states NVX has a $340,000 five-year bank loan. A rise of 0.75 percentage points adds 0.75% Ã— $340,000 = $2,550 a year if the loan is variable-rate; if the rate is fixed, the direct effect is nil. Higher base rates could also raise the cost of future borrowing for the $640,000 expansion and make consumers more cautious about fashion clothing manufacturing and retail spending.

Minimum wage increase (6.2%, to $14.02 per hour): With a workforce of 96, this raises wage costs in the partly hourly-paid fulfilment and store roles. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay rates, so no defensible annual wage bill can be invented. The only honest yardstick is the productivity already derivable: 80,000 units Ã· 96 staff = 833 units per worker. A wage rise is absorbable only if productivity holds near that level or output grows, otherwise unit labour costs rise and the $4.80 contribution per unit shrinks.

Input cost inflation (11.3% in cotton and fabric): NVX's variable cost is $7.20 a unit and the insert does not decompose it, so the only defensible bound is to apply the full rise: 11.3% Ã— $7.20 = $0.814 a unit, which at 80,000 units is about $65,088 a year (80,000 Ã— $0.814). Even a smaller effect would cut the $4.80 contribution and threaten the $640,000 investment; the $$0.50 premium from the survey can recover only part of it.

Conclusion: The 11.3% rise in cotton and fabric costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds on every one of the 80,000 units sold, directly erodes the $4.80 contribution that justifies the $640,000 expansion, and is only partly offset by the premium. The interest rise is smaller ($2,550 at most, and possibly nil), and the wage impact, though unavoidable, can be managed through the 833-unit productivity the business already achieves.

mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of Northvale Apparel with a well-justified judgment on which has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
